chart.Keywords: trend, time-series, line, growth, timeline, progress
chart.When to Use: Data has a time axis; user needs to observe rise/fall trends or rate of change over a continuous period
chart.When NOT to Use: Fewer than 4 data points (use stat card); more than 6 series (visual noise); no time dimension exists
chart.Data Volume Threshold: <1000 pts: SVG; ≥1000 pts: Canvas + downsampling; >10000: aggregate to intervals
chart.Color Guidance: Primary: #0080FF. Multiple series: distinct colors + distinct line styles. Fill: 20% opacity
chart.Accessibility Notes: Differentiate series by line style (solid/dashed/dotted) not color alone. Add pattern overlays for colorblind users.
chart.A11y Fallback: Dashed/dotted lines per series; togglable data table with timestamps and values

chart.Keywords: compare, categories, bar, comparison, ranking
chart.When to Use: Comparing discrete categories by magnitude; ranking or ordering is the core insight; categories ≤ 15
chart.When NOT to Use: Categories > 15 (use table or search); data has time dimension (use line); showing proportions (use waffle/stacked)
chart.Data Volume Threshold: <20 categories: vertical bar; 20–50: horizontal bar; >50: paginated table
chart.Color Guidance: Each bar: distinct color. Grouped: same hue family. Always sort descending by value
chart.Accessibility Notes: Value labels on each bar by default. Sort control for user reordering.
chart.A11y Fallback: Value labels always visible; provide CSV export

chart.Keywords: part-to-whole, pie, donut, percentage, proportion, share
chart.When to Use: ≤5 categories; one dominant segment vs rest; emphasis on visual proportion over exact values
chart.When NOT to Use: Categories > 5; slice differences < 5% (visually indistinguishable); user needs precise values; accessibility-first context
chart.Data Volume Threshold: Max 6 slices; beyond that switch to stacked bar 100%
chart.Color Guidance: 5–6 max colors. Contrasting palette. Largest slice at 12 o'clock. Always label slices with %
chart.Accessibility Notes: Pie charts fail WCAG for colorblind users. Slices rely on color alone. Avoid as primary chart in a11y contexts.
chart.A11y Fallback: Must provide stacked bar alternative + percentage data table as mandatory fallback

chart.Keywords: correlation, distribution, scatter, relationship, pattern, cluster
chart.When to Use: Exploring relationship between two continuous variables; identifying clusters or outliers in a dataset
chart.When NOT to Use: Variables are categorical (use grouped bar); fewer than 20 points (patterns aren't meaningful); mobile-primary context
chart.Data Volume Threshold: <500 pts: SVG; 500–5000: Canvas at 0.6–0.8 opacity; >5000: hexbin or aggregate first
chart.Color Guidance: Color axis: gradient (blue → red). Bubble size: relative to 3rd variable. Opacity: 0.6–0.8 to show density
chart.Accessibility Notes: Provide data table alternative. Combine color + shape distinction for colorblind users.
chart.A11y Fallback: Data table with correlation coefficient annotation; shape markers (circle/square/triangle) per group

chart.Keywords: heatmap, heat-map, intensity, density, matrix, calendar
chart.When to Use: Showing intensity/density across a 2D grid; time-based patterns (e.g., activity by hour × day)
chart.When NOT to Use: Fewer than 20 cells (use bar); user needs to read exact values; colorblind users without pattern fallback
chart.Data Volume Threshold: Up to 10,000 cells efficiently; beyond that aggregate; calendar heatmap: 365 cells max per SVG
chart.Color Guidance: Gradient: Cool (blue) to Hot (red). Divergent scale for ±data. Always include numeric color legend
chart.Accessibility Notes: Pattern overlay for colorblind users. Numerical value on hover. Legend must include scale ticks.
chart.A11y Fallback: Numerical overlay on hover; downloadable grid table with row/column labels

chart.Keywords: geographic, map, location, region, geo, spatial, choropleth
chart.When to Use: Data has a regional/location dimension; spatial distribution is the core insight for the user
chart.When NOT to Use: Regions have very different sizes making visual comparison misleading (use bar); mobile-primary context
chart.Data Volume Threshold: <1000 regions: SVG; ≥1000: Canvas/WebGL (Deck.gl); global maps: tile-based rendering
chart.Color Guidance: Single color gradient per region group. Categorized colors for discrete types. Legend with clear scale breaks
chart.Accessibility Notes: Include text labels for major regions. Provide keyboard navigation between regions.
chart.A11y Fallback: Region text labels; sortable data table by region name and value; keyboard-navigable regions

chart.Keywords: funnel, flow, conversion, drop-off, pipeline, stages
chart.When to Use: Sequential multi-stage process; showing conversion or drop-off rates between defined stages
chart.When NOT to Use: Stages aren't sequential; values don't decrease monotonically (use bar); fewer than 3 stages
chart.Data Volume Threshold: 3–8 stages optimal; beyond 8 stages group minor steps into 'Other'
chart.Color Guidance: Stages: single color gradient (start → end). Show conversion % between each stage. Highlight biggest drop
chart.Accessibility Notes: Explicit conversion % as text per stage. Stage labels always visible. Linear list view as fallback.
chart.A11y Fallback: Provide linear list view with stage name + count + drop-off %; keyboard traversal

chart.Keywords: performance, target, kpi, gauge, goal, threshold, progress
chart.When to Use: Single KPI measured against a defined target or threshold; dashboard summary context
chart.When NOT to Use: No target or benchmark exists; comparing multiple KPIs at once (use bullet chart grid)
chart.Data Volume Threshold: Single metric per gauge; for 3+ KPIs use bullet chart grid layout
chart.Color Guidance: Performance: Red → Yellow → Green gradient. Target: marker line. Threshold zones clearly differentiated
chart.Accessibility Notes: Always show numerical value + % of target as text beside chart. Never rely on color position alone.
chart.A11y Fallback: Numerical value + % of target shown as visible text; ARIA live region for real-time updates

chart.Keywords: forecast, prediction, confidence, band, projection, estimate
chart.When to Use: Historical data + model predictions; communicating uncertainty range to non-technical stakeholders
chart.When NOT to Use: No historical baseline; prediction confidence is too low to be useful; audience is not data-literate
chart.Data Volume Threshold: Keep historical window to 30–90 days for readability; forecast horizon ≤ 30% of visible x-axis range
chart.Color Guidance: Actual: solid line #0080FF. Forecast: dashed #FF9500. Confidence band: 15% opacity fill same hue
chart.Accessibility Notes: Toggle between actual-only and forecast views. Legend must distinguish lines beyond color (solid vs dashed).
chart.A11y Fallback: Toggle actual/forecast independently; legend labels must include line-style description

chart.Keywords: anomaly, outlier, spike, alert, detection, monitoring, deviation
chart.When to Use: Monitoring a time-series for outliers; alerting users to unexpected spikes or dips in operational data
chart.When NOT to Use: Anomalies are predefined categories (use bar with highlight); real-time context without a pause control
chart.Data Volume Threshold: Stream at ≤60fps with Canvas; batch: up to 10,000 pts; mark anomalies as a separate data layer
chart.Color Guidance: Normal: #0080FF solid line. Anomaly marker: #FF0000 circle + filled. Alert band: #FFF3CD background zone
chart.Accessibility Notes: Use shape marker (not color only) for anomaly points. Add text annotation per anomaly event.
chart.A11y Fallback: Text alert annotation per anomaly; anomaly summary list panel alongside chart

chart.Keywords: hierarchy, nested, treemap, parent, children, breakdown, drill
chart.When to Use: Showing size relationships within a hierarchy; overview of proportional structure (e.g., budget breakdown)
chart.When NOT to Use: Hierarchy depth > 3 levels (too complex to read); user needs to compare sibling values precisely
chart.Data Volume Threshold: <200 nodes: SVG; 200–1000: Canvas; >1000: paginate or pre-filter before rendering
chart.Color Guidance: Parent nodes: distinct hues. Children: lighter shades of same hue. White separator borders: 2–3px
chart.Accessibility Notes: Poor baseline accessibility. Always provide table alternative as primary view. Label all large areas.
chart.A11y Fallback: Collapsible tree table as primary view; treemap as supplementary visual only

chart.Keywords: flow, process, sankey, distribution, source, target, transfer
chart.When to Use: Showing how quantities flow between nodes; multi-source multi-target distribution
chart.When NOT to Use: Flow directions form loops (use network graph); fewer than 3 source-target pairs; mobile-primary context
chart.Data Volume Threshold: <50 flows: SVG; ≥50: Canvas; >200 flows: aggregate minor flows into 'Other' node
chart.Color Guidance: Gradient from source to target color. Flow opacity: 0.4–0.6. Node labels always visible
chart.Accessibility Notes: Structural flow charts cannot be conveyed by color alone. Provide flow table. Avoid on mobile.
chart.A11y Fallback: Flow table (Source → Target → Value); keyboard-traversable node list with tab stops

chart.Keywords: waterfall, cumulative, variance, incremental, bridge, delta
chart.When to Use: Showing how individual positive/negative components add up to a final total (e.g., P&L, budget variance)
chart.When NOT to Use: Changes are not additive; more than 12 bars (readability breaks); audience expects a simple total
chart.Data Volume Threshold: 4–12 bars optimal; beyond 12 aggregate minor items into a single 'Other' bar
chart.Color Guidance: Increases: #4CAF50. Decreases: #F44336. Start total: #2196F3. End total: #0D47A1. Running total line: dashed
chart.Accessibility Notes: Color + directional arrow icon per bar (not color alone). Labels on every bar.
chart.A11y Fallback: Table with running total column; directional arrow icons per row

chart.Keywords: radar, spider, multi-variable, attributes, dimensions, comparison
chart.When to Use: Comparing multiple entities across the same fixed set of attributes (e.g., product feature comparison)
chart.When NOT to Use: Axes > 8 (unreadable); values need precise comparison (use grouped bar); audience unfamiliar with radar charts
chart.Data Volume Threshold: 2–3 datasets maximum per chart; 5–8 axes; beyond 8 axes switch to parallel coordinates
chart.Color Guidance: Single dataset: #0080FF at 20% fill. Multiple: distinct hues with 30% fill. Border: full opacity
chart.Accessibility Notes: Limit axes to 5–8. Always provide grouped bar chart alternative for precise reading.
chart.A11y Fallback: Grouped bar chart as mandatory alternative; include raw data table

chart.Keywords: stock, trading, ohlc, candlestick, finance, price, volume
chart.When to Use: Financial time-series with Open/High/Low/Close data; trading or investment product context only
chart.When NOT to Use: Non-financial audience; no OHLC data available (use line chart); accessibility-first context
chart.Data Volume Threshold: Real-time: Canvas required. Historical: paginate by time range. Max 500 candles visible at once
chart.Color Guidance: Bullish: #26A69A. Bearish: #EF5350. Volume bars: 40% opacity below. Body fill vs hollow for OHLC style
chart.Accessibility Notes: Provide OHLC data table. Colorblind: use fill vs outline pattern (bullish = filled, bearish = hollow).
chart.A11y Fallback: OHLC data table with sortable columns; numeric summary panel (daily change %)

chart.Keywords: network, graph, nodes, edges, connections, relationships, force
chart.When to Use: Mapping connections between entities; network topology or social graph exploration context
chart.When NOT to Use: Node count > 500 without clustering pre-applied; user needs precise connection counts; mobile context
chart.Data Volume Threshold: ≤100 nodes: SVG; 101–500: Canvas; >500: must apply clustering/LOD before rendering
chart.Color Guidance: Node types: categorical colors. Edges: #90A4AE at 60% opacity. Highlight path: #F59E0B
chart.Accessibility Notes: Fundamentally inaccessible without alternative. Never use as sole representation. Always provide list alternative.
chart.A11y Fallback: Adjacency list table (Node A → Node B → Weight); hierarchical tree view when structure allows

chart.Keywords: distribution, statistical, spread, median, outlier, quartile, boxplot
chart.When to Use: Showing spread, median, and outliers of a dataset; comparing distributions across multiple groups
chart.When NOT to Use: Fewer than 20 data points per group (distribution is not meaningful); audience unfamiliar with statistical charts
chart.Data Volume Threshold: Any sample size; aggregated representation so rendering is ⚡ Excellent at any volume
chart.Color Guidance: Box fill: #BBDEFB. Border: #1976D2. Median line: #D32F2F bold. Outlier dots: #F44336
chart.Accessibility Notes: Include stats summary table. Annotate outlier count in chart subtitle.
chart.A11y Fallback: Stats summary table (min / Q1 / median / Q3 / max / mean); outlier count annotation

chart.Keywords: bullet, compact, kpi, dashboard, target, benchmark, range
chart.When to Use: Dashboard with multiple KPIs side by side; space-constrained contexts where a gauge is too large
chart.When NOT to Use: Single KPI with emphasis (use gauge); data has no defined target range; fewer than 3 KPIs
chart.Data Volume Threshold: Ideal for 3–10 bullet charts in a grid; scales to any count efficiently
chart.Color Guidance: Qualitative ranges: #FFCDD2 / #FFF9C4 / #C8E6C9 (bad/ok/good). Performance bar: #1976D2. Target: black 3px marker
chart.Accessibility Notes: All values always visible as text. Color ranges are labeled with text thresholds not color alone.
chart.A11y Fallback: Numerical values always visible (not hover-only); color ranges labeled with threshold text

chart.Keywords: waffle, percentage, proportion, progress, filled, grid
chart.When to Use: Showing what fraction of a whole is filled; percentage progress in a visually engaging and accessible format
chart.When NOT to Use: More than 5 categories (use stacked bar); exact values matter over visual proportion; very tight space
chart.Data Volume Threshold: 10×10 grid standard (100 cells); for > 5 categories switch to stacked 100% bar
chart.Color Guidance: 3–5 categories max. 2–3px gap between cells. Each category a distinct accessible color pair
chart.Accessibility Notes: Better than pie for accessibility. Percentage text label always visible. Each cell has aria-label.
chart.A11y Fallback: Percentage text always visible; grid cells labeled with aria-label value; provide legend

chart.Keywords: sunburst, hierarchy, nested, proportion, radial, circle
chart.When to Use: Exploring nested proportions where both hierarchy and relative size matter (e.g., org spend breakdown)
chart.When NOT to Use: More than 3 hierarchy levels (outer rings become unreadable); precision matters over overview; mobile
chart.Data Volume Threshold: <100 nodes: SVG; 100–500: Canvas; >500: filter to top N before rendering
chart.Color Guidance: Center to outer: darker to lighter hue. Each level 15–20% lighter. Contrasting border between sectors
chart.Accessibility Notes: Poor accessibility beyond 2 levels. Mandatory table alternative required for any production use.
chart.A11y Fallback: Collapsible indented list with percentages; breadcrumb trail for current drill-down state

chart.Keywords: root cause, decomposition, tree, hierarchy, drill-down, ai-split, attribution
chart.When to Use: Decomposing a metric into contributing factors; AI-assisted analysis or BI drill-down scenarios
chart.When NOT to Use: No clear parent-child causal relationship; audience expects a summary rather than exploration
chart.Data Volume Threshold: Up to 5 levels deep; limit visible nodes to 20 per level for readability; lazy-load deeper levels
chart.Color Guidance: Positive impact nodes: #2563EB. Negative impact nodes: #EF4444. Neutral connectors: #94A3B8
chart.Accessibility Notes: Keyboard-navigable expand/collapse. Screen reader announces node value and % contribution.
chart.A11y Fallback: Keyboard expand/collapse tree; screen reader announces node label + value + % impact

chart.Keywords: 3d, spatial, immersive, terrain, molecular, volumetric, point-cloud
chart.When to Use: Scientific/engineering context where Z-axis carries essential info not expressible in 2D
chart.When NOT to Use: 2D projection conveys the same insight; mobile context; accessibility-required environments; standard business dashboards
chart.Data Volume Threshold: WebGL required. Deck.gl: up to 1M points. Three.js: LOD required beyond 50,000 pts
chart.Color Guidance: Depth cues: lighting and shading. Z-axis: color gradient (cool → warm). Transparent overlapping: opacity 0.4
chart.Accessibility Notes: 3D spatial charts are fundamentally inaccessible. Must not be used as primary chart type in any product UI.
chart.A11y Fallback: Mandatory 2D projection view + data table; do not use as primary chart type in product UI

chart.Keywords: streaming, real-time, ticker, live, velocity, pulse, monitoring
chart.When to Use: Live monitoring dashboards; IoT/ops data updating at ≥1 Hz; user needs current value at a glance
chart.When NOT to Use: Update frequency < 1/min (use periodic-refresh line chart); flashing content without reduced-motion support
chart.Data Volume Threshold: Canvas/WebGL required. Buffer last 60–300s of data. Downsample older data on scroll
chart.Color Guidance: Current pulse: #00FF00 (dark theme) or #0080FF (light theme). History: fading opacity. Grid: dark background
chart.Accessibility Notes: Pause/resume control required. Current value as large visible text KPI. Respect prefers-reduced-motion.
chart.A11y Fallback: Pause/resume button required; current value shown as large text KPI; prefers-reduced-motion: freeze animation

chart.Keywords: sentiment, emotion, nlp, opinion, feeling, text-analysis
chart.When to Use: NLP output visualization; exploratory analysis of text corpus sentiment; frequency-weighted keyword overview
chart.When NOT to Use: Precise values matter (word size is inherently imprecise); screen-reader context; corpus < 50 items
chart.Data Volume Threshold: 50–5000 terms optimal. Beyond 5000: apply top-N filtering before render. Avoid on mobile
chart.Color Guidance: Positive: #22C55E. Negative: #EF4444. Neutral: #94A3B8. Word size maps to frequency
chart.Accessibility Notes: Word clouds fail screen readers. Never use as sole output of NLP analysis. Always pair with list view.
chart.A11y Fallback: Sortable list view by frequency with sentiment label column; word cloud as supplementary only

chart.Keywords: process, mining, variants, path, bottleneck, log, event
chart.When to Use: Analyzing event logs to visualize actual process flows; identifying bottlenecks and deviations in ops/product funnels
chart.When NOT to Use: No event log data available; audience expects a static flowchart (use diagram tool); node count > 100 without pre-filtering
chart.Data Volume Threshold: <30 nodes: SVG; 30–100: Canvas; >100: apply variant filtering (top 80% of cases) before rendering
chart.Color Guidance: Happy path: #10B981 thick line. Deviations: #F59E0B thin line. Bottleneck nodes: #EF4444 fill
chart.Accessibility Notes: Complex graphs are hard to navigate. Provide path summary text. Highlight top 3 bottlenecks as annotations.
chart.A11y Fallback: Path summary table (variant → frequency → avg duration); top 3 bottlenecks as text annotation panel

ux.Description: Anchor links should scroll smoothly to target section
ux.Do: Use scroll-behavior: smooth on html element

ux.Description: Fixed nav should not obscure content
ux.Do: Add padding-top to body equal to nav height
ux.Don't: Let nav overlap first section content

ux.Description: Current page/section should be visually indicated
ux.Do: Highlight active nav item with color/underline
ux.Don't: No visual feedback on current location

ux.Description: Users expect back to work predictably
URLs should reflect current state for sharing
Show user location in site hierarchy
ux.Do: Use for sites with 3+ levels of depth

ux.Description: Too many animations cause distraction and motion sickness
ux.Do: Animate 1-2 key elements per view maximum

ux.Description: Animations should feel responsive not sluggish
ux.Don't: Use animations longer than 500ms for UI
Leave UI frozen with no feedback

ux.Description: Hover effects don't work on touch devices
ux.Don't: Rely only on hover for important actions

ux.Description: Some CSS properties trigger expensive repaints
ux.Do: Use transform and opacity for animations
Use ease-out for entering ease-in for exiting

ux.Description: Stacking context conflicts cause hidden elements
Hidden overflow can clip important content
ux.Do: Test all content fits within containers

ux.Description: Fixed elements can overlap or be inaccessible
ux.Do: Account for safe areas and other fixed elements
ux.Code Example Good: Fixed nav + fixed bottom with gap

ux.Do: Understand what creates new stacking context
ux.Don't: Expect z-index to work across contexts

ux.Description: Layout shift when content loads is jarring

gsap.Keywords: hover, button, opacity, lift, press feedback
gsap.Framework Notes: Bind on mouseenter/mouseleave; in React wrap in a ref + useEffect (or onMouseEnter/onMouseLeave props directly calling gsap.to)
gsap.Do: Keep displacement under 2px so it reads as feedback not motion
gsap.Don't: Don't animate layout-affecting props (width/height/margin) on hover
gsap.Performance Notes: Runs on transform/opacity only so it stays on the compositor thread

gsap.Keywords: hover, card, scale, tilt, cursor feedback
gsap.GSAP Snippet: gsap.to(el, { y: -4, scale: 1.02, boxShadow: '0 12px 24px rgba(0,0,0,0.12)', duration: 0.25, ease: 'power2.out' });
gsap.Framework Notes: Use gsap.quickTo(el, 'y') for cards with many hover targets to avoid re-creating tweens every event
gsap.Do: Pair with a matching mouseleave tween that reverses the same properties
gsap.Don't: Don't leave the hover state stuck if the pointer leaves fast; always attach the reverse tween
gsap.Performance Notes: quickTo() avoids GC churn on lists with 20+ hoverable cards

gsap.GSAP Snippet: const xTo = gsap.quickTo(el, 'x', { duration: 0.4, ease: 'elastic.out(1,0.4)' }); const yTo = gsap.quickTo(el, 'y', { duration: 0.4, ease: 'elastic.out(1,0.4)' }); el.addEventListener('mousemove', (e) => { const r = el.getBoundingClientRect(); xTo((e.clientX - r.left - r.width/2) * 0.3); yTo((e.clientY - r.top - r.height/2) * 0.3); });
gsap.Framework Notes: Debounce is not needed since quickTo interpolates; remove listeners on component unmount in React/Vue to avoid leaks
gsap.Do: Clamp the pull strength (e.g. * 0.3) so the element never fully leaves its hit box
gsap.Don't: Don't apply magnetic effect to more than 1-2 focal elements per screen; it becomes noisy
gsap.Performance Notes: Use will-change: transform on the target element for smoother compositing

gsap.Keywords: scroll, fade in, reveal, on view
gsap.GSAP Snippet: gsap.from(el, { opacity: 0, y: 12, duration: 0.35, ease: 'power1.out', scrollTrigger: { trigger: el, start: 'top 90%', toggleActions: 'play none none reverse' } });
gsap.Framework Notes: Requires the ScrollTrigger plugin registered once via gsap.registerPlugin(ScrollTrigger)
gsap.Do: Keep the y offset small (8-16px) so it reads as a fade, not a slide
gsap.Don't: Don't reveal below-the-fold content needed for SEO/crawlers as invisible-by-default without a no-JS fallback
gsap.Performance Notes: toggleActions 'play none none reverse' avoids re-triggering on every scroll direction change

gsap.Keywords: scroll, slide up, staggered section, reveal
gsap.GSAP Snippet: gsap.from(el.children, { opacity: 0, y: 24, duration: 0.5, stagger: 0.08, ease: 'power2.out', scrollTrigger: { trigger: el, start: 'top 85%' } });
gsap.Framework Notes: In React use useGSAP(() => {...}, { scope: containerRef }) from @gsap/react to auto-cleanup on unmount
gsap.Do: Scope the ScrollTrigger to the section container so it doesn't re-scan the whole page
gsap.Don't: Don't stagger more than ~8 children; beyond that the last items feel laggy
gsap.Performance Notes: Set scroller/markers: false in production; markers is dev-only

gsap.GSAP Snippet: gsap.timeline({ scrollTrigger: { trigger: section, start: 'top top', end: '+=150%', scrub: 1, pin: true } }).from('.headline', { opacity: 0, y: 40 }).to('.bg-layer', { yPercent: -20 }, '<');
gsap.Framework Notes: Pinning needs the section to have deterministic height; recalc ScrollTrigger.refresh() after images/fonts load
gsap.Do: Use scrub: true or a small number (0.5-1.5) instead of instant jumps so it feels tied to the scrollbar
gsap.Don't: Don't pin more than 1-2 sections per page; excessive pinning fights native scroll feel and hurts mobile UX
gsap.Performance Notes: Pinning forces layout reflow; test on mid-tier mobile devices, not just desktop

gsap.Framework Notes: Select items with a stable class/data-attribute (not array index) so re-renders in React don't break targeting
gsap.Do: Keep per-item stagger delay small (0.02-0.04s) for lists longer than 10 items
gsap.Don't: Don't stagger by more than 0.1s per item on long lists; total reveal time becomes sluggish
gsap.Performance Notes: For virtualized lists, only animate items currently mounted in the DOM

gsap.GSAP Snippet: gsap.from('.grid-item', { opacity: 0, scale: 0.92, y: 16, duration: 0.4, stagger: { each: 0.06, from: 'start', grid: 'auto' }, ease: 'back.out(1.4)' });
gsap.Framework Notes: grid: 'auto' lets GSAP infer rows/columns from a CSS grid layout for a natural wave stagger
gsap.Do: Combine with from: 'center' for a bento-grid layout to draw the eye inward first
gsap.Don't: Don't use back.out on dense data tables; the overshoot reads as sloppy on informational UI
gsap.Performance Notes: Group DOM writes; avoid interleaving layout reads (getBoundingClientRect) between staggered tweens

gsap.Keywords: stagger, wave, text reveal, split text
gsap.GSAP Snippet: const split = new SplitText(headline, { type: 'chars' }); gsap.from(split.chars, { opacity: 0, y: 20, rotateX: -40, duration: 0.6, stagger: 0.015, ease: 'expo.out' });
gsap.Framework Notes: SplitText is a GSAP Club/paid plugin; confirm license before shipping and provide a plain fade fallback if unavailable
gsap.Do: Revert SplitText on unmount/cleanup (split.revert()) to restore original text nodes for accessibility tools
gsap.Don't: Don't split-animate long paragraphs; reserve for short headlines (under ~8 words)
gsap.Performance Notes: Splitting text creates one element per character; keep it to headline-length copy only for DOM size

gsap.GSAP Snippet: gsap.to(main, { opacity: 0, duration: 0.2, onComplete: () => { navigate(); gsap.fromTo(main, { opacity: 0 }, { opacity: 1, duration: 0.2 }); } });
gsap.Framework Notes: Pair with the router's transition hooks (Next.js App Router transitions, React Router's useNavigate, Vue Router's beforeEach/afterEach)
gsap.Do: Preload the destination route's critical assets before the exit tween finishes
gsap.Don't: Don't block navigation on animation; cap exit duration at ~250ms so the app never feels unresponsive
gsap.Performance Notes: Exit animation should always resolve faster than entrance (asymmetric timing) so back/forward feels snappy

gsap.GSAP Snippet: const tl = gsap.timeline(); tl.to('.transition-overlay', { yPercent: 0, duration: 0.4, ease: 'power2.inOut' }).call(navigate).to('.transition-overlay', { yPercent: -100, duration: 0.4, ease: 'power2.inOut', delay: 0.1 });
gsap.Framework Notes: Keep the overlay element mounted at the layout root (outside the page component) so it survives the route swap
gsap.Do: Show a lightweight loading indicator if the destination route's data fetch outlasts the overlay
gsap.Don't: Don't tie the overlay's reveal directly to data-fetch completion without a max-wait timeout; a slow API stalls the whole transition
gsap.Performance Notes: Prefer CSS transform (yPercent) over top/left to keep the overlay animation on the compositor thread

gsap.GSAP Snippet: const state = Flip.getState('.hero-image'); navigate(); Flip.from(state, { duration: 0.6, ease: 'expo.inOut', absolute: true, zIndex: 100 });
gsap.Framework Notes: Requires the GSAP Flip plugin; the 'from' and 'to' route must render the same element with a shared data-flip-id
gsap.Do: Verify the shared element exists in both DOM states before calling Flip.from to avoid a silent no-op
gsap.Don't: Don't use shared-element transitions across more than one element pair per navigation; compounding Flips are hard to time correctly
gsap.Performance Notes: Flip recalculates layout (FLIP technique) so test on low-end devices for jank

gsap.GSAP Snippet: gsap.to('.bg-layer', { yPercent: 10, ease: 'none', scrollTrigger: { trigger: section, scrub: true } });
gsap.Framework Notes: Apply parallax to background/decorative layers only, never to text or interactive controls
gsap.Do: Keep the yPercent delta small (5-15) so foreground and background never desync distractingly
gsap.Don't: Don't parallax body copy; it hurts reading comfort and can trigger motion sickness
gsap.Performance Notes: will-change: transform on the parallax layer only; remove it after scroll settles to free GPU memory

gsap.GSAP Snippet: gsap.utils.toArray('.parallax-layer').forEach((layer, i) => { gsap.to(layer, { yPercent: (i + 1) * -8, ease: 'none', scrollTrigger: { trigger: layer.parentElement, scrub: 0.5 } }); });
gsap.Framework Notes: Layer count beyond 3-4 has diminishing visual return and multiplies scroll-listener cost
gsap.Do: Vary speed per layer (background slowest, foreground fastest) to sell the depth illusion
gsap.Don't: Don't let parallax layers overflow their container; clip with overflow: hidden on the wrapper
gsap.Performance Notes: Batch all layers under one ScrollTrigger container where possible instead of one per layer

gsap.Framework Notes: Kill the loop tween (tween.kill()) as soon as real content mounts to avoid orphaned repeating animations
gsap.Do: Use a CSS gradient background-position sweep rather than opacity pulsing; reads as 'loading' more clearly
gsap.Don't: Don't run more than one shimmer loop per skeleton group; sync them under one timeline so the wave reads as a single unit
gsap.Performance Notes: repeat: -1 tweens are cheap but must be explicitly killed on unmount or they leak in SPA route changes

gsap.GSAP Snippet: gsap.timeline({ repeat: -1 }).to('.loader-dot', { y: -8, duration: 0.4, stagger: { each: 0.15, yoyo: true, repeat: 1 } });
gsap.Framework Notes: Wrap the whole loop timeline in useGSAP with { revertOnUpdate: false } in React so it isn't rebuilt every render
gsap.Do: Cap total loop duration under ~1.5s so long waits don't feel like the UI froze on a single beat
gsap.Don't: Don't use elaborate loaders for sub-300ms waits; they flash and feel worse than no indicator
gsap.Performance Notes: Pause the timeline (tl.pause()) when the loading tab/view is not visible to save CPU on background tabs

react.Description: Move await into branches where actually used to avoid blocking unused code paths
react.Do: Move await operations into branches where they're needed
react.Don't: Await at top of function blocking all branches

react.Code Example Bad: const data = await fetch(); if (skip) return { skipped: true }

react.Don't: Wait for unrelated data before starting dependent fetch
react.Code Example Good: await all({ user() {}, config() {}, profile() { return fetch((await this.$.user).id) } })
react.Code Example Bad: const [user, config] = await Promise.all([...]); const profile = await fetchProfile(user.id)

react.Description: In API routes start independent operations immediately even if not awaited yet

threejs.Description: Always use Three.js r128 from cdnjs. It is the stable CDN baseline. Never use a floating 'latest' URL — it silently breaks when the CDN updates without warning.
threejs.Do: Pin to the exact r128 cdnjs URL in every HTML file
threejs.Don't: Use unpkg@latest or any unversioned CDN URL that can silently update
threejs.Code Good: <script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/three.js/r128/three.min.js"></script>
threejs.Code Bad: <script src="https://unpkg.com/three@latest"></script>

threejs.Guideline: CapsuleGeometry Does Not Exist in r128
threejs.Description: THREE.CapsuleGeometry was introduced in r142. Using it on the r128 CDN throws 'CapsuleGeometry is not a constructor' and crashes the entire scene. Build a capsule from primitives instead.
threejs.Do: Build a capsule from CylinderGeometry plus two SphereGeometry end caps
threejs.Don't: Call THREE.CapsuleGeometry on r128 — it is undefined and throws immediately
threejs.Code Good: const body = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.CylinderGeometry(0.5, 0.5, 1, 16), mat); const topCap = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.SphereGeometry(0.5, 16, 8), mat); const botCap = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.SphereGeometry(0.5, 16, 8), mat); topCap.position.y = 0.5; botCap.position.y = -0.5; const group = new THREE.Group(); group.add(body, topCap, botCap);
threejs.Code Bad: const cap = new THREE.CapsuleGeometry(0.5, 1, 4, 8); // TypeError: CapsuleGeometry is not a constructor on r128

threejs.Description: OrbitControls is NOT bundled in the core Three.js r128 CDN file. It lives in examples/js and must be loaded from a separate cdnjs script tag. THREE.OrbitControls is undefined without it.
threejs.Do: Load the OrbitControls script from cdnjs examples path before your scene script
threejs.Don't: Expect THREE.OrbitControls to exist after loading only the core Three.js CDN script
threejs.Code Good: <!-- Load AFTER core Three.js script --> <script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/three.js/r128/examples/js/controls/OrbitControls.min.js"></script>
threejs.Code Bad: <!-- Core only loaded — OrbitControls undefined --> <script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/three.js/r128/three.min.js"></script>

threejs.Description: When OrbitControls cannot be loaded implement spherical orbit using mousedown/mousemove/mouseup. The key is rotating in spherical coordinates so both horizontal AND vertical drag work correctly.
threejs.Do: Rotate camera in spherical coordinates so both axes respond correctly to drag
threejs.Don't: Move camera.position.x directly — vertical drag is silently ignored and the orbit is incorrect
threejs.Code Good: let dragging = false; let prev = { x: 0, y: 0 }; const radius = camera.position.length(); let theta = 0; let phi = Math.PI / 2; canvas.addEventListener('mousedown', () => dragging = true); canvas.addEventListener('mouseup', () => dragging = false); canvas.addEventListener('mousemove', e => { if (!dragging) return; theta -= (e.clientX - prev.x) * 0.005; phi = Math.max(0.1, Math.min(Math.PI - 0.1, phi - (e.clientY - prev.y) * 0.005)); camera.position.set(radius * Math.sin(phi) * Math.sin(theta), radius * Math.cos(phi), radius * Math.sin(phi) * Math.cos(theta)); camera.lookAt(scene.position); prev = { x: e.clientX, y: e.clientY }; });
threejs.Code Bad: let dragging = false; let prev = { x: 0, y: 0 }; canvas.addEventListener('mousemove', e => { if (!dragging) return; camera.position.x += (e.clientX - prev.x) * 0.005; camera.lookAt(scene.position); prev = { x: e.clientX, y: e.clientY }; }); // BUG: Y-drag ignored; orbit is a horizontal slide not a sphere

threejs.Description: When using a bundler import Three.js as an ES module. When using CDN the THREE global is already available — do not import it again. Mixing both loads Three.js twice and causes subtle runtime errors.
threejs.Do: Match import style to build environment: ESM import for bundlers; rely on the window.THREE global for CDN pages
threejs.Don't: Mix a CDN script tag with an ES module import in the same file
threejs.Code Good: // Bundler project (Vite / webpack): import * as THREE from 'three'; // CDN project — no import needed; THREE is already global after the script tag
threejs.Code Bad: <!-- CDN script --> <script src="r128.cdn"></script> <script type="module"> import * as THREE from 'three'; // loads Three.js twice — version mismatch risk </script>

threejs.Description: Create one WebGLRenderer instance for the lifetime of the page. Multiple renderers compete for the browser GPU context limit (8–16 contexts) and cause context-lost errors especially on mobile.
threejs.Do: Reuse a single renderer and swap scene content instead of recreating the renderer
threejs.Don't: Create a new renderer on each component mount or scene transition
threejs.Code Good: const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ antialias: true, alpha: true }); renderer.setPixelRatio(Math.min(window.devicePixelRatio, 2)); renderer.setSize(canvas.clientWidth, canvas.clientHeight); // renderer lives for the page lifetime
threejs.Code Bad: function showScene() { const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer(); document.body.appendChild(renderer.domElement); } showScene(); showScene(); // two GPU contexts — crashes on mobile

threejs.Description: Cap devicePixelRatio at 2. Retina displays report 3x or higher. Going from 2x to 3x multiplies pixel count by 2.25x with no visible quality improvement at normal viewing distance.
threejs.Do: Apply Math.min(window.devicePixelRatio, 2) — cap is at 2 not at 3
threejs.Don't: Pass window.devicePixelRatio directly without any cap
threejs.Code Good: renderer.setPixelRatio(Math.min(window.devicePixelRatio, 2));
threejs.Code Bad: renderer.setPixelRatio(window.devicePixelRatio); // 3x display = 9 pixels per CSS pixel = 2.25x GPU cost for zero quality gain

threejs.Description: Set alpha:true on the renderer and control the background color through CSS rather than a renderer clear color. This composites the canvas correctly over any HTML content behind it.
threejs.Do: Set alpha:true on renderer and let body or a parent div provide the background color
threejs.Don't: Set a solid renderer clear color when the canvas must composite over HTML behind it
threejs.Code Good: const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ alpha: true }); renderer.setClearColor(0x000000, 0); // fully transparent canvas // body { background: #0d0d0d; } handles the visible color
threejs.Code Bad: renderer.setClearColor(0x111827); // fully opaque — HTML behind the canvas is blocked

threejs.Description: Always update camera.aspect and call camera.updateProjectionMatrix() inside every resize handler. A stale aspect ratio causes the entire scene to appear stretched or squashed horizontally.
threejs.Do: Update camera.aspect then call updateProjectionMatrix() on every resize
threejs.Don't: Let aspect ratio become stale after the browser window changes size
threejs.Code Good: window.addEventListener('resize', () => { camera.aspect = canvas.clientWidth / canvas.clientHeight; camera.updateProjectionMatrix(); renderer.setSize(canvas.clientWidth, canvas.clientHeight); });
threejs.Code Bad: // No resize handler — scene stretches to fill a wider window without correcting the projection

threejs.Description: Use a field of view between 45 and 75 degrees. Below 45 creates compressed telephoto distortion. Above 90 creates visible fisheye distortion at frame edges.
threejs.Do: Start at 75 for general interactive scenes; use 45–55 for product close-ups
threejs.Don't: Use FOV above 90 or below 30 without a deliberate artistic reason
threejs.Code Good: const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(75, aspect, 0.1, 1000); // general const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(50, aspect, 0.1, 1000); // product shot
threejs.Code Bad: const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(120, aspect, 0.1, 1000); // fisheye distortion at all edges

threejs.Description: Always set an explicit camera position and call camera.lookAt() before the first render. The default camera at the origin pointing down -Z makes subjects at arbitrary coordinates invisible or tiny.
threejs.Do: Set camera.position.set() and camera.lookAt() to frame the subject before the first render
threejs.Don't: Leave the camera at default position (0 0 0) with no lookAt — subject may be behind the camera or microscopic
threejs.Code Good: camera.position.set(0, 1.5, 5); camera.lookAt(new THREE.Vector3(0, 0, 0));
threejs.Code Bad: // No position or lookAt set — subject at y:2 is behind or above the default camera view

threejs.Description: Use OrbitControls for model viewers and exploratory scenes where the user needs free-look. Use a GSAP scroll-driven camera rig for product reveals or storytelling where the camera path must stay fixed.
threejs.Do: Match camera control approach to the UX intent of the scene
threejs.Don't: Use OrbitControls for a scripted reveal — users can orbit away from the reveal before it completes
threejs.Code Good: // Scroll storytelling — GSAP controls the path: gsap.to(camera.position, { z: 2, scrollTrigger: { trigger: '.scene', scrub: 1 } }); // Free-look model viewer — OrbitControls: const controls = new THREE.OrbitControls(camera, renderer.domElement); controls.enableDamping = true; // call controls.update() in animate()
threejs.Code Bad: // Scripted product reveal: const controls = new THREE.OrbitControls(camera, renderer.domElement); // user can rotate away before the animation completes

threejs.Description: Creating a new geometry inside animate() allocates a fresh GPU buffer every frame and exhausts VRAM within seconds. Create all geometry exactly once before the loop starts. Use attribute mutation if positions must change per frame.
threejs.Do: Create all geometry before the animation loop; mutate BufferAttribute arrays in-place if needed
threejs.Don't: Call any new XxxGeometry() constructor inside the animation loop
threejs.Code Good: const geo = new THREE.SphereGeometry(1, 32, 32); // created once const mesh = new THREE.Mesh(geo, mat); scene.add(mesh); const clock = new THREE.Clock(); function animate() { requestAnimationFrame(animate); mesh.rotation.y += clock.getDelta() * 0.8; // delta time renderer.render(scene, camera); }
threejs.Code Bad: function animate() { requestAnimationFrame(animate); const geo = new THREE.BoxGeometry(1, 1, 1); // NEW GPU buffer every frame — VRAM exhaustion }

threejs.Description: When multiple objects share the same shape create one geometry instance and pass it to every Mesh. Each Mesh gets its own transform and material while all share a single GPU buffer.
threejs.Do: Create one geometry and pass the same reference to every Mesh constructor
threejs.Don't: Create a separate identical geometry inside a loop for each object
threejs.Code Good: const geo = new THREE.BoxGeometry(1, 1, 1); // one GPU buffer for (let i = 0; i < 200; i++) { const m = new THREE.Mesh(geo, mat); m.position.set(Math.random() * 10, 0, Math.random() * 10); scene.add(m); }
threejs.Code Bad: for (let i = 0; i < 200; i++) { const geo = new THREE.BoxGeometry(1, 1, 1); // 200 separate GPU buffers scene.add(new THREE.Mesh(geo, mat)); }

threejs.Description: Call geometry.dispose() and material.dispose() and texture.dispose() for every texture map when removing objects from the scene. Three.js never releases GPU resources automatically — they stay in VRAM until explicitly freed.
threejs.Do: Dispose of geometry + material + every texture map before calling scene.remove()
threejs.Don't: Call scene.remove() alone without any dispose calls
threejs.Code Good: function removeMesh(mesh) { scene.remove(mesh); mesh.geometry.dispose(); if (mesh.material.map) mesh.material.map.dispose(); if (mesh.material.normalMap) mesh.material.normalMap.dispose(); mesh.material.dispose(); }
threejs.Code Bad: scene.remove(mesh); // geometry and all texture maps stay in GPU VRAM forever

threejs.Description: Use the minimum segment count that achieves the desired silhouette quality. Hero objects: 32–64 segments. Background objects: 8–16. Particle stand-ins: 6–8. High counts on background geometry waste GPU draw calls with zero visible benefit.
threejs.Do: Apply a tiered segment budget based on the visual priority of each object in the scene
threejs.Don't: Default every sphere and cylinder to 64+ segments regardless of its role
threejs.Code Good: const bgSphere = new THREE.SphereGeometry(0.5, 8, 8); // background const heroSphere = new THREE.SphereGeometry(1, 64, 64); // foreground product
threejs.Code Bad: const particleSphere = new THREE.SphereGeometry(0.1, 64, 64); // 64 segments × 1000 particles = massive overdraw

threejs.Description: For any custom shape use BufferGeometry with setAttribute('position' ...) and a Float32Array. The legacy THREE.Geometry class was removed in r125 and throws ReferenceError in r128.
threejs.Do: Use THREE.BufferGeometry with a Float32Array position attribute for custom vertex data
threejs.Don't: Reference or instantiate the removed THREE.Geometry class
threejs.Code Good: const geo = new THREE.BufferGeometry(); geo.setAttribute('position', new THREE.BufferAttribute(new Float32Array(vertices), 3)); geo.setAttribute('normal', new THREE.BufferAttribute(new Float32Array(normals), 3));
threejs.Code Bad: const geo = new THREE.Geometry(); geo.vertices.push(new THREE.Vector3(0, 0, 0)); // ReferenceError: Geometry is not defined in r128

threejs.Description: MeshBasicMaterial ignores all lights and is significantly cheaper — use it for UI overlays HUDs and flat-colored decorative elements. MeshStandardMaterial is PBR-accurate and requires lights. Never use StandardMaterial where BasicMaterial suffices.
threejs.Do: Use MeshBasicMaterial for any object that does not need lighting; use MeshStandardMaterial for physical objects
threejs.Don't: Apply MeshStandardMaterial to flat UI elements that never receive light — lights still run for them
threejs.Code Good: const uiMat = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ color: 0xffffff }); // no lighting cost const physMat = new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x4f46e5, roughness: 0.4, metalness: 0.6 });
threejs.Code Bad: const mat = new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0xffffff }); // on a 2D HUD card — lighting calculation runs with no visual benefit

threejs.Description: Share one material instance across all meshes that have identical properties. Call mat.clone() only when individual meshes genuinely need different property values. Duplicate materials waste GPU VRAM.
threejs.Do: Assign the same material reference to all meshes with identical visual properties
threejs.Don't: Create a new material inside a loop for objects that look identical
threejs.Code Good: const mat = new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x4f46e5, roughness: 0.5 }); meshA.material = mat; meshB.material = mat; meshC.material = mat; // one GPU material
threejs.Code Bad: for (const m of meshes) { m.material = new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x4f46e5 }); } // N redundant GPU materials

threejs.Description: Textures are the single largest consumer of GPU VRAM in most Three.js scenes. Call texture.dispose() when switching scenes or removing objects — Three.js does not garbage-collect GPU resources automatically.
threejs.Do: Track all loaded textures and call dispose() on each one during scene teardown or on object removal
threejs.Don't: Load textures without any cleanup path — they persist in VRAM for the entire page lifetime
threejs.Code Good: const tex = new THREE.TextureLoader().load('img.jpg'); mesh.material.map = tex; // on teardown: tex.dispose(); mesh.material.dispose();
threejs.Code Bad: const tex = new THREE.TextureLoader().load('img.jpg'); scene.remove(mesh); // tex occupies GPU VRAM until page reload

threejs.Description: Any scene using MeshStandardMaterial or MeshPhongMaterial requires at minimum one AmbientLight (fill) and one DirectionalLight (shading direction). Without both the objects render as solid black — the material is there but no light reaches it.
threejs.Do: Add AmbientLight for fill and DirectionalLight for shading whenever PBR or Phong materials are used
threejs.Don't: Use MeshStandardMaterial without adding any lights to the scene
threejs.Code Good: scene.add(new THREE.AmbientLight(0xffffff, 0.4)); const dirLight = new THREE.DirectionalLight(0xffffff, 1.0); dirLight.position.set(5, 10, 7.5); scene.add(dirLight);
threejs.Code Bad: const mesh = new THREE.Mesh(geo, new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x4f46e5 })); scene.add(mesh); // renders completely black — no lights in scene

threejs.Description: renderer.shadowMap.enabled = true must be set before any castShadow or receiveShadow flags. Without it the shadow map is never allocated and all shadow flags are silently ignored.
threejs.Do: Set renderer.shadowMap.enabled = true first then set castShadow and receiveShadow on lights and meshes
threejs.Don't: Set castShadow on a light or mesh without enabling renderer.shadowMap.enabled — shadows never render
threejs.Code Good: renderer.shadowMap.enabled = true; renderer.shadowMap.type = THREE.PCFSoftShadowMap; dirLight.castShadow = true; dirLight.shadow.mapSize.width = 2048; dirLight.shadow.mapSize.height = 2048; heroMesh.castShadow = true; ground.receiveShadow = true;
threejs.Code Bad: dirLight.castShadow = true; heroMesh.castShadow = true; // renderer.shadowMap.enabled never set — shadows silently do not render

threejs.Description: Shadow map rendering redraws the entire scene from the light's perspective every frame. Enable castShadow only on the primary directional light and receiveShadow only on hero meshes and the ground plane.
threejs.Do: Enable shadows only on the key light and the most important meshes
threejs.Don't: Enable castShadow and receiveShadow on every object in the scene including particles
threejs.Code Good: renderer.shadowMap.enabled = true; renderer.shadowMap.type = THREE.PCFSoftShadowMap; dirLight.castShadow = true; heroMesh.castShadow = true; ground.receiveShadow = true; // particles and background meshes: no shadow flags
threejs.Code Bad: for (const m of allMeshes) { m.castShadow = true; m.receiveShadow = true; } // shadow map pass over particle system — expensive with no visible gain

threejs.Description: MeshBasicMaterial completely ignores all scene lights. Adding lights solely to illuminate BasicMaterial objects wastes a light pass on every frame with zero visible effect.
threejs.Do: Omit lights entirely when every material in the scene is MeshBasicMaterial
threejs.Don't: Add AmbientLight and DirectionalLight to a scene that uses only MeshBasicMaterial
threejs.Code Good: // Scene uses only MeshBasicMaterial — no lights needed const mat = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ color: 0x00ffff }); const mesh = new THREE.Mesh(geo, mat); scene.add(mesh); // MeshBasicMaterial is always fully lit by definition
threejs.Code Bad: scene.add(new THREE.AmbientLight(0xffffff, 1.0)); // wasted per-frame light pass — BasicMaterial ignores it entirely

threejs.Description: Create exactly one Raycaster instance outside all event handlers. Store mouse coordinates in pointermove (cheap). Call setFromCamera and intersectObjects together inside the animate() loop — once per frame instead of once per mouse event.
threejs.Do: Create one Raycaster; store mouse in pointermove; call setFromCamera + intersectObjects inside animate()
threejs.Don't: Create a new THREE.Raycaster() inside a mousemove handler or call setFromCamera inside the event listener
threejs.Code Good: const raycaster = new THREE.Raycaster(); const mouse = new THREE.Vector2(); canvas.addEventListener('pointermove', e => { // only store coords — no raycasting here mouse.x = (e.clientX / canvas.clientWidth) * 2 - 1; mouse.y = -(e.clientY / canvas.clientHeight) * 2 + 1; }); // setFromCamera and intersectObjects run once per frame in animate()
threejs.Code Bad: window.addEventListener('mousemove', e => { const rc = new THREE.Raycaster(); // new allocation per event rc.setFromCamera(mouse, camera); rc.intersectObjects(targets, true); // fires 200+ times/sec });

threejs.Description: Raycasting requires mouse in Normalized Device Coordinates: X from -1 (left) to +1 (right) and Y from +1 (top) to -1 (bottom). The Y axis is inverted relative to screen space. A missing negation on Y causes all raycasts to miss or hit the wrong objects.
threejs.Do: Apply the full NDC formula — including the negation on the Y axis
threejs.Don't: Forget to negate Y — raycasting appears to work but hits objects mirrored vertically
threejs.Code Good: mouse.x = (e.clientX / canvas.clientWidth) * 2 - 1; mouse.y = -(e.clientY / canvas.clientHeight) * 2 + 1; // Y is INVERTED
threejs.Code Bad: mouse.x = (e.clientX / canvas.clientWidth) * 2 - 1; mouse.y = (e.clientY / canvas.clientHeight) * 2 - 1; // BUG: Y not negated — raycasting is mirrored

threejs.Description: Call raycaster.setFromCamera(mouse camera) and then raycaster.intersectObjects(targets true) inside the animate() loop. setFromCamera must come before intersectObjects every frame — without it the raycaster uses a stale ray direction.
threejs.Do: Call setFromCamera then intersectObjects in order inside every animate() frame
threejs.Don't: Call intersectObjects without calling setFromCamera first — the raycaster uses a stale or zero ray
threejs.Code Good: function animate() { requestAnimationFrame(animate); raycaster.setFromCamera(mouse, camera); // update ray direction first const hits = raycaster.intersectObjects(targets, true); // then test intersections if (hits.length > 0) { document.body.style.cursor = 'pointer'; } else { document.body.style.cursor = 'auto'; } renderer.render(scene, camera); }
threejs.Code Bad: function animate() { requestAnimationFrame(animate); const hits = raycaster.intersectObjects(targets, true); // BUG: setFromCamera never called — stale ray — hits is always empty renderer.render(scene, camera); }

threejs.Guideline: Recursive Flag for Groups and GLTF
threejs.Description: Pass true as the second argument to intersectObjects when testing Groups or GLTF loaded models. Geometry lives on child Mesh objects — without recursive:true the parent group is tested but has no geometry and hits is always empty.
threejs.Do: Use intersectObjects(targets true) for Groups or any loaded model
threejs.Don't: Raycast against a parent Group without the recursive flag
threejs.Code Good: const hits = raycaster.intersectObjects(scene.children, true); // catches all descendant meshes
threejs.Code Bad: const hits = raycaster.intersectObjects([modelGroup]); // recursive defaults to false — misses all children

threejs.Description: Set document.body.style.cursor = 'pointer' when intersections are found and reset to 'auto' when none are found. Without cursor feedback users cannot discover that 3D objects are interactive.
threejs.Do: Update cursor to pointer on hit; reset to auto on miss in the same animate loop block
threejs.Don't: Run raycasting and read hits without ever updating the cursor style
threejs.Code Good: if (hits.length > 0) { document.body.style.cursor = 'pointer'; } else { document.body.style.cursor = 'auto'; }
threejs.Code Bad: raycaster.setFromCamera(mouse, camera); raycaster.intersectObjects(targets, true); // hits ignored — cursor never changes — objects feel non-interactive

threejs.Description: Drive the render loop exclusively with requestAnimationFrame or renderer.setAnimationLoop(). Never use setInterval or setTimeout — they are not synchronized to the display refresh rate and keep running when the tab is hidden draining battery.
threejs.Do: Use requestAnimationFrame or renderer.setAnimationLoop() as the sole render loop driver
threejs.Don't: Use setInterval or setTimeout for render timing
threejs.Code Good: function animate() { requestAnimationFrame(animate); renderer.render(scene, camera); } animate();
threejs.Code Bad: setInterval(() => renderer.render(scene, camera), 16); // not display-synced; runs at full speed even when tab is hidden

threejs.Description: Use THREE.Clock and clock.getDelta() for all time-based motion. A hardcoded increment like += 0.01 runs at 2x speed on 120Hz displays and at unpredictable speed when frames drop under load. CRITICAL: call getDelta() exactly ONCE per animate() frame and store the result in a local dt variable. getDelta() resets the internal clock on every call — a second call in the same frame always returns ~0, silently breaking any animation block that uses it.
threejs.Do: Call clock.getDelta() once at the top of animate(); store result in dt; reuse dt everywhere in that frame
threejs.Don't: Call clock.getDelta() more than once per frame or inside a helper called from animate()
threejs.Code Good: const clock = new THREE.Clock(); function animate() { requestAnimationFrame(animate); const dt = clock.getDelta(); // called ONCE — reuse dt below mesh.rotation.y += dt * 0.8; particles.rotation.y += dt * 0.1; // reuse dt, not a second getDelta() renderer.render(scene, camera); }
threejs.Code Bad: function animate() { requestAnimationFrame(animate); mesh.rotation.y += 0.01; // 0.01 rad/frame — runs 2x faster on 120Hz than on 60Hz }

threejs.Description: Use value += (target - value) * alpha each frame to smoothly interpolate toward a moving target. An alpha of 0.03–0.1 produces organic easing for camera follow pointer-tracking and hover scale effects without requiring GSAP.
threejs.Do: Apply the lerp formula each frame with a small alpha for smooth organic motion
threejs.Don't: Snap a value directly to the target producing an instant jarring jump
threejs.Code Good: // In animate(): cameraTargetX = mouse.x * 3; camera.position.x += (cameraTargetX - camera.position.x) * 0.05; camera.position.y += (cameraTargetY - camera.position.y) * 0.05; camera.lookAt(scene.position);
threejs.Code Bad: // In animate(): camera.position.x = mouse.x * 3; // instant snap — jarring with no easing

threejs.Description: Use GSAP timelines for any animation with more than two sequential steps or for scroll-linked camera paths. GSAP timelines can be paused reversed and scrubbed — far more maintainable than boolean state machines.
threejs.Do: Use GSAP timelines for sequences with more than two steps and for scroll-driven animations
threejs.Don't: Implement multi-step sequences with boolean flags and manual frame counters
threejs.Code Good: const tl = gsap.timeline({ defaults: { ease: 'power2.out' } }); tl.from(mesh.position, { y: -3, duration: 1 }) .to(mesh.rotation, { y: Math.PI, duration: 1 }, '-=0.3') .to(camera.position, { z: 2, duration: 1.5 });
threejs.Code Bad: let step = 0; let t = 0; function animate() { if (step === 0 && (t += 0.01) >= 1) step = 1; } // grows unmanageable with 3+ steps

threejs.Guideline: Pause Render Loop on Tab Hidden
threejs.Description: Use renderer.setAnimationLoop() as the loop driver so you can pass null to pause and a function to resume. Continuous rendering in a hidden tab wastes CPU GPU and battery with no user benefit.
threejs.Do: Use renderer.setAnimationLoop(animate) to drive the loop; pass null to pause on visibilitychange
threejs.Don't: Drive with internal requestAnimationFrame and never stop the loop when the tab is hidden
threejs.Code Good: renderer.setAnimationLoop(animate); // use setAnimationLoop as the driver — not requestAnimationFrame inside animate function animate() { const dt = clock.getDelta(); renderer.render(scene, camera); } document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', () => { if (document.hidden) renderer.setAnimationLoop(null); else renderer.setAnimationLoop(animate); });
threejs.Code Bad: function animate() { requestAnimationFrame(animate); // self-referencing RAF cannot be stopped externally renderer.render(scene, camera); } animate(); // runs forever in background tab — drains battery

threejs.Description: Load GSAP from its own CDN script tag before your scene script. In bundler projects install via npm and import. GSAP is a completely separate library from Three.js — never try to import it from the Three.js package.
threejs.Do: Load GSAP CDN before the scene script; or npm install gsap and import separately
threejs.Don't: Import gsap from three or expect it to be defined without a separate load
threejs.Code Good: <!-- CDN: load GSAP before your scene script --> <script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/gsap/3.12.2/gsap.min.js"></script> <!-- Bundler: --> // import gsap from 'gsap'; import { ScrollTrigger } from 'gsap/ScrollTrigger';
threejs.Code Bad: import gsap from 'three'; // undefined — GSAP has nothing to do with Three.js

threejs.Description: Call gsap.registerPlugin(ScrollTrigger) once at the top of your script before any scrollTrigger config object. Without registration the ScrollTrigger name is undefined and the tween throws immediately.
threejs.Do: Call gsap.registerPlugin(ScrollTrigger) as the first line before any gsap.to/from/timeline with scrollTrigger
threejs.Don't: Include scrollTrigger config in gsap.to() calls without first registering the plugin
threejs.Code Good: gsap.registerPlugin(ScrollTrigger); gsap.to(camera.position, { z: 2, scrollTrigger: { trigger: '.hero-section', scrub: 1 } });
threejs.Code Bad: gsap.to(mesh.position, { scrollTrigger: { trigger: '.section', scrub: true } }); // TypeError: ScrollTrigger is not a constructor — not registered

threejs.Description: GSAP can tween any numeric JavaScript property including mesh.position.x mesh.rotation.y and material.opacity. No wrapper or adaptor is needed. Note: to tween material.opacity the material must have transparent:true set before the tween starts.
threejs.Do: Pass Three.js object properties directly to gsap.to(); set transparent:true before tweening opacity
threejs.Don't: Use a plain proxy object then manually copy values to Three.js properties every frame
threejs.Code Good: gsap.to(mesh.rotation, { y: Math.PI * 2, duration: 2, ease: 'power1.inOut' }); mesh.material.transparent = true; // required before tweening opacity gsap.to(mesh.material, { opacity: 0, duration: 1 });
threejs.Code Bad: const tw = { v: 0 }; gsap.to(tw, { v: Math.PI * 2, onUpdate: () => mesh.rotation.y = tw.v }); // unnecessary proxy wrapper

threejs.Description: Use scrub:true or scrub:1 to link camera movement continuously to scroll position as a 0–1 ratio. scrub:1 adds a 1-second lag for cinematic smoothness. onEnter/onLeave fire only once and create jarring snaps — not the right tool for a camera path.
threejs.Do: Use scrub:1 for any scroll-controlled camera movement
threejs.Don't: Use onEnter or onLeave callbacks for camera motion — they snap instead of scrubbing
threejs.Code Good: gsap.registerPlugin(ScrollTrigger); gsap.to(camera.position, { x: 5, y: 2, z: 0, ease: 'none', scrollTrigger: { trigger: '.canvas-wrapper', start: 'top top', end: 'bottom bottom', scrub: 1 } });
threejs.Code Bad: gsap.to(camera.position, { z: 0, scrollTrigger: { trigger: '.section', onEnter: () => {} } }); // fires once at scroll threshold — not a continuous scrub

threejs.Description: Use THREE.InstancedMesh when rendering 50 or more identical objects. It submits all N transforms in one draw call instead of N draw calls and reduces CPU-GPU communication overhead dramatically.
threejs.Do: Use InstancedMesh for any group of 50+ meshes sharing the same geometry and material
threejs.Don't: Create 50+ separate Mesh objects with the same geometry and material
threejs.Code Good: const COUNT = 500; const iMesh = new THREE.InstancedMesh(geo, mat, COUNT); const matrix = new THREE.Matrix4(); for (let i = 0; i < COUNT; i++) { matrix.setPosition(Math.random()*10, Math.random()*10, Math.random()*10); iMesh.setMatrixAt(i, matrix); } iMesh.instanceMatrix.needsUpdate = true; scene.add(iMesh);
threejs.Code Bad: for (let i = 0; i < 500; i++) { scene.add(new THREE.Mesh(geo, mat)); } // 500 separate draw calls per frame

threejs.Description: Enable ACESFilmicToneMapping and sRGBEncoding on the renderer for accurate perceptual color. Without tone mapping colors appear washed out or over-saturated. These are renderer properties set after construction and take effect immediately.
threejs.Do: Set renderer.toneMapping and renderer.outputEncoding after construction for all production scenes
threejs.Don't: Leave tone mapping and output encoding at defaults when the scene targets realistic visuals
threejs.Code Good: renderer.toneMapping = THREE.ACESFilmicToneMapping; renderer.toneMappingExposure = 1.0; renderer.outputEncoding = THREE.sRGBEncoding; // correct for r128
threejs.Code Bad: const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer(); // defaults: NoToneMapping + LinearEncoding — colors appear flat and incorrect

threejs.Description: The antialias option can only be set at WebGLRenderer construction time. Setting renderer.antialias after construction has absolutely no effect — the WebGL context is already created without it. Decide before instantiating.
threejs.Do: Set antialias:true inside the WebGLRenderer constructor options object
threejs.Don't: Construct the renderer without antialias then try to enable it by assigning the property
threejs.Code Good: const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ antialias: true, alpha: true }); // antialias baked into the WebGL context
threejs.Code Bad: const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer(); renderer.antialias = true; // no effect — context created without AA — edges remain aliased

threejs.Guideline: FogExp2 for Depth and Far Culling
threejs.Description: Use scene.fog to create atmospheric depth. As a secondary benefit objects that disappear into fog before the far plane stop contributing to draw calls — useful in scenes with large view distances.
threejs.Do: Add FogExp2 to scenes with view distances above 100 units for both visual atmosphere and implicit far culling
threejs.Don't: Ignore fog in scenes with far:1000+ and many distant objects that contribute tiny pixels per draw call
threejs.Code Good: scene.fog = new THREE.FogExp2(0x0a0a0a, 0.02); // exponential — density feels more natural than linear
threejs.Code Bad: // far: 2000 with no fog — hundreds of distant objects too small to see still cost draw calls per frame

threejs.Guideline: BufferGeometry Plus Points for Particle Systems
threejs.Description: Build all particle systems with BufferGeometry plus a Float32Array position attribute rendered as Points. Never use individual Mesh objects as particles — they cannot scale past a few hundred with good performance.
threejs.Do: Use Points plus BufferGeometry for all particle effects
threejs.Don't: Create hundreds of individual Mesh objects to simulate a particle system
threejs.Code Good: const COUNT = 3000; const geo = new THREE.BufferGeometry(); const pos = new Float32Array(COUNT * 3); for (let i = 0; i < COUNT * 3; i++) pos[i] = (Math.random() - 0.5) * 20; geo.setAttribute('position', new THREE.BufferAttribute(pos, 3)); const particles = new THREE.Points(geo, new THREE.PointsMaterial({ size: 0.05, color: 0xffffff })); scene.add(particles);
threejs.Code Bad: for (let i = 0; i < 500; i++) { scene.add(new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.SphereGeometry(0.05, 8, 8), mat)); } // 500 separate draw calls per frame

threejs.Description: Start particle systems at 1000–3000 particles. Beyond 50000 causes sustained frame drops on mid-range mobile. Always test on a real device before increasing the count — desktop and mobile GPU performance ratios can be 10:1.
threejs.Do: Start at 3000 particles and profile on actual mobile hardware before raising the limit
threejs.Don't: Set particle count at 100000 or higher without any mobile profiling
threejs.Code Good: const COUNT = 3000; // safe mobile baseline — profile before going higher const pos = new Float32Array(COUNT * 3);
threejs.Code Bad: const COUNT = 150000; // 60fps on desktop — 8fps on a mid-range Android phone

threejs.Description: After mutating any BufferAttribute array values per frame you must set geometry.attributes.position.needsUpdate = true so Three.js re-uploads the changed buffer to the GPU. Without it the GPU still uses the old data and particles appear completely frozen.
threejs.Do: Set needsUpdate = true on the position attribute after every per-frame mutation of the array
threejs.Don't: Mutate the Float32Array values without flagging needsUpdate — positions update in JS but not on the GPU
threejs.Code Good: // In animate(): const pos = geo.attributes.position.array; for (let i = 0; i < pos.length; i += 3) { pos[i + 1] += Math.sin(clock.getElapsedTime() + i) * 0.001; // Y component } geo.attributes.position.needsUpdate = true; // GPU re-upload
threejs.Code Bad: // In animate(): pos[1] += 0.001; // JS array updated — GPU buffer is stale — particles do not move

threejs.Description: Size the renderer and camera to the canvas element's clientWidth and clientHeight — not window.innerWidth and innerHeight. This is correct when the canvas is inside a flex or grid container that does not fill the full viewport.
threejs.Do: Use canvas.clientWidth and canvas.clientHeight for all renderer and camera sizing
threejs.Don't: Hardcode renderer size to window.innerWidth/innerHeight when the canvas may be inside a container
threejs.Code Good: renderer.setSize(canvas.clientWidth, canvas.clientHeight); camera.aspect = canvas.clientWidth / canvas.clientHeight; camera.updateProjectionMatrix();
threejs.Code Bad: renderer.setSize(window.innerWidth, window.innerHeight); // wrong when canvas lives inside a sidebar or grid column

threejs.Description: Use ResizeObserver on the canvas container instead of the window resize event. ResizeObserver fires when the container element changes size independently of the browser window — common in split-pane layouts and sidebar collapsing.
threejs.Do: Attach ResizeObserver to the canvas parent element for accurate container-aware resize detection
threejs.Don't: Use only window.addEventListener('resize') for canvas sizing when the canvas is not fullscreen
threejs.Code Good: const ro = new ResizeObserver(entries => { const { width, height } = entries[0].contentRect; renderer.setSize(width, height); camera.aspect = width / height; camera.updateProjectionMatrix(); }); ro.observe(canvas.parentElement);
threejs.Code Bad: window.addEventListener('resize', () => { renderer.setSize(window.innerWidth, window.innerHeight); }); // misses container-only resize events in split-pane UIs

threejs.Description: Add touchstart and touchmove listeners alongside mouse events so the scene remains interactive on mobile. Normalize touch coordinates to the same NDC range as mouse events and pass passive:false on touchmove if you call preventDefault.
threejs.Do: Handle both mouse and touch input for any interactive 3D scene
threejs.Don't: Add only mouse event listeners and leave touch users with no interaction
threejs.Code Good: canvas.addEventListener('touchmove', e => { e.preventDefault(); const t = e.touches[0]; mouse.x = (t.clientX / canvas.clientWidth) * 2 - 1; mouse.y = -(t.clientY / canvas.clientHeight) * 2 + 1; }, { passive: false }); canvas.addEventListener('touchstart', e => { e.preventDefault(); }, { passive: false });
threejs.Code Bad: canvas.addEventListener('mousemove', handleMouse); // touch events unhandled — mobile users get no interaction

threejs.Description: Check window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)') before starting any auto-rotation, particle animation, or camera movement. Users who enable this OS preference have motion sickness or vestibular disorders. IMPORTANT: reading .matches once at page load is a one-time snapshot — if the user changes their OS accessibility setting mid-session the scene will not react. Attach a 'change' listener to the MediaQueryList so noMotion stays in sync at runtime.
threejs.Do: Use matchMedia.addEventListener('change') to keep noMotion reactive; gate all auto-animation on the live value
threejs.Don't: Read .matches once at startup and never update it — the scene ignores mid-session OS setting changes
threejs.Code Good: const mq = window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)'); let noMotion = mq.matches; mq.addEventListener('change', e => { noMotion = e.matches; }); // In animate(): if (!noMotion) { mesh.rotation.y += dt * 0.8; particles.rotation.y += dt * 0.1; }
threejs.Code Bad: const noMotion = window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches; // one-time snapshot — mid-session OS change is ignored entirely

threejs.Description: Add role='img' and a descriptive aria-label to renderer.domElement after appending it to the DOM. Screen readers receive no information from a WebGL canvas — the aria-label is the only description they can announce to users.
threejs.Do: Set role='img' and a meaningful aria-label on renderer.domElement before or after appending it
threejs.Don't: Append the canvas to the DOM with no accessibility attributes — invisible to screen readers
threejs.Code Good: renderer.domElement.setAttribute('role', 'img'); renderer.domElement.setAttribute('aria-label', 'Interactive 3D product viewer. Drag to rotate. Scroll to zoom.'); document.body.appendChild(renderer.domElement);
threejs.Code Bad: document.body.appendChild(renderer.domElement); // bare canvas — screen readers announce nothing

threejs.Description: For production use Three.js via npm plus Vite. You get full tree-shaking reduced bundle size access to the complete examples/jsm library including OrbitControls GLTFLoader and EffectComposer and TypeScript support.
threejs.Do: Use npm install three plus Vite or Webpack for any production client-facing project
threejs.Don't: Serve raw CDN script tags in a production application that needs tree-shaking or TypeScript
threejs.Code Good: npm install three gsap // then in your JS: import * as THREE from 'three'; import { OrbitControls } from 'three/examples/jsm/controls/OrbitControls.js'; import { GLTFLoader } from 'three/examples/jsm/loaders/GLTFLoader.js';
threejs.Code Bad: <!-- In a Vite/React production build: --> <script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/three.js/r128/three.min.js"></script> // no tree-shaking — entire Three.js ships

threejs.Description: Load 3D models using GLTFLoader and traverse gltf.scene to configure castShadow receiveShadow and material overrides on all child Mesh nodes. Calling scene.add(gltf.scene) alone silently skips all shadow and material configuration.
threejs.Do: Use GLTFLoader and traverse the entire gltf.scene graph to set up shadows and materials on every Mesh child
threejs.Don't: Load a GLTF model and pass gltf.scene directly to scene.add without traversing child meshes
threejs.Code Good: import { GLTFLoader } from 'three/examples/jsm/loaders/GLTFLoader.js'; const loader = new GLTFLoader(); loader.load('model.glb', gltf => { gltf.scene.traverse(child => { if (child.isMesh) { child.castShadow = true; child.receiveShadow = true; } }); scene.add(gltf.scene); });
threejs.Code Bad: loader.load('model.glb', gltf => { scene.add(gltf.scene); // shadows and material setup silently skipped on all children });

threejs.Description: Use THREE.LOD to automatically swap high-detail and low-detail geometry as objects move closer or farther from the camera. This maintains frame rate in scenes with many objects spread across a large depth range.
threejs.Do: Use THREE.LOD to reduce triangle count on distant objects automatically
threejs.Don't: Render the same high-polygon geometry for every object regardless of its distance from the camera
threejs.Code Good: const lod = new THREE.LOD(); lod.addLevel(highDetailMesh, 0); // used when < 15 units away lod.addLevel(medDetailMesh, 15); // 15–50 units lod.addLevel(lowDetailMesh, 50); // 50+ units scene.add(lod);
threejs.Code Bad: scene.add(highDetailMesh); // 64k-triangle mesh rendered at full cost whether 1 unit or 100 units from camera
